title: 17: Alcohols and Phenols
summary: A chapter overview of alcohol and phenol chemistry, including classification, properties, preparation, reactions, oxidation, and phenol chemistry. This is the neutral fallback reading link when a more specific article is not selected.

title: 17.1: Naming Alcohols and Phenols
summary: Explains the structural distinction between alcohols and phenols and the primary, secondary, and tertiary classification based on the carbon that bears the hydroxyl group. Covers naming alcohols and phenols.

title: 17.2: Properties of Alcohols and Phenols
summary: Alcohols and phenols hydrogen-bond and are weak acids and bases. Phenols are much more acidic than alcohols because phenoxide is resonance-stabilized; electron-withdrawing and electron-donating substituents change phenol acidity.

title: 17.3: Preparation of Alcohols: A Review
section: Preparation of alcohols from alkenes and other groups
summary: Reviews alcohol synthesis from alkenes, alkyl halides, aldehydes, ketones, esters, and related functional groups. Hydroboration-oxidation gives syn, anti-Markovnikov hydration, while oxymercuration-demercuration gives Markovnikov hydration.

title: 17.4: Alcohols from Carbonyl Compounds: Reduction
section: Reduction of carbonyl compounds to alcohols
summary: Explains reduction of aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, and esters to alcohols. Aldehydes give primary alcohols, ketones give secondary alcohols, and stronger hydride reagents can reduce carboxylic-acid derivatives.

title: 17.5: Alcohols from Carbonyl Compounds: Grignard Reagents
summary: Grignard reagents add as carbon nucleophiles to carbonyl compounds. Addition to formaldehyde gives primary alcohols, aldehydes give secondary alcohols, and ketones or esters give tertiary alcohols. Esters receive two additions before acidic work-up.

title: 17.6: Reactions of Alcohols
section: Substitution, dehydration, and esterification of alcohols
summary: Covers conversion of alcohols into alkyl halides or tosylates, acid-catalysed dehydration to alkenes, and ester formation. The mechanism and outcome depend on alcohol substitution and reaction conditions.

title: 13.13: Reactions with Phosphorus Halides and Thionyl Chloride
section: Conversion of alcohols to alkyl halides
summary: Phosphorus halides and thionyl chloride convert alcohols into alkyl halides by first making the hydroxyl group a better leaving group. PBr3 and SOCl2 are useful for avoiding strongly acidic conditions and generally proceed through backside substitution with inversion.

title: 17.7: Oxidation of Alcohols
section: Oxidation of primary, secondary, and tertiary alcohols
summary: Primary alcohols oxidize to aldehydes or carboxylic acids depending on conditions; secondary alcohols oxidize to ketones. Tertiary alcohols normally do not react with common oxidants because oxidation would require carbon-carbon bond cleavage.

title: 10.5: Preparing Alkyl Halides from Alcohols
section: Lucas test and conversion of alcohols to alkyl halides
summary: Lucas reagent is concentrated hydrochloric acid and zinc chloride. It converts alcohols to alkyl chlorides: tertiary alcohols react immediately and turn cloudy, secondary alcohols react more slowly, and primary alcohols do not react significantly at room temperature.

title: The Triiodomethane (Iodoform) Reaction
section: Iodoform test for alcohols and methyl ketones
summary: The iodoform test detects the CH3CH(OH) group in alcohols and methyl ketones. A positive result is pale-yellow triiodomethane precipitate. Ethanol is the only primary alcohol that gives this reaction; appropriate secondary alcohols do, but tertiary alcohols do not.

title: 17.10: Reactions of Phenols
section: Electrophilic substitution and oxidation of phenols
summary: The phenolic hydroxyl group strongly activates the benzene ring and directs electrophilic aromatic substitution to ortho and para positions. Phenols undergo halogenation, nitration, sulfonation, and related reactions; oxidation gives quinones rather than ordinary alcohol oxidation products.

title: 17.9: Phenols and Their Uses
section: Preparation of phenols: Dow and cumene processes
summary: Phenol can be made industrially from chlorobenzene by the Dow process or from cumene. In the cumene process, oxidation gives cumene hydroperoxide, which undergoes acid treatment to form phenol and acetone.

title: Preparation of Esters
section: Esterification of alcohols and phenols; aspirin connection
summary: Alcohols and phenols form esters with acylating reagents. Phenol reacts more slowly than an alcohol, but conversion to phenoxide increases its reactivity. Acylation of the phenolic hydroxyl group in salicylic-acid chemistry is the key esterification idea used in aspirin synthesis.

title: 26.1: Aryl Oxygen Compounds
section: Kolbe-Schmitt and Reimer-Tiemann reactions of phenols
summary: The Kolbe-Schmitt reaction carboxylates sodium phenoxide with carbon dioxide to give hydroxybenzoic-acid products, commonly ortho under the stated conditions. Reimer-Tiemann reaction of phenoxide with chloroform in base forms salicylaldehyde through dichlorocarbene chemistry.

title: 15.3: The Williamson Ether Synthesis
summary: Williamson ether synthesis is an SN2 reaction between an alkoxide or phenoxide nucleophile and an alkyl halide. A primary alkyl halide is preferred because secondary and tertiary substrates increasingly favour E2 elimination with strong alkoxide base.

title: 18.3: Reactions of Ethers: Acidic Cleavage
summary: Ethers are cleaved by strong hydrogen halides. The pathway depends on the substituents: aryl-alkyl ethers produce phenol plus alkyl halide because aryl carbon does not undergo ordinary SN1 or SN2 cleavage.

title: 14.9: Reactions of Epoxides with Grignard and Organolithium Reagents
summary: Grignard and organolithium reagents open epoxide rings by the same SN2-type pathway as base-promoted epoxide opening. Attack occurs at the less hindered carbon; ethylene oxide extends the carbon chain by two carbons and gives a primary alcohol after protonation.

title: 11.2: Pinacol Rearrangement
summary: The pinacol rearrangement is an acid- or Lewis-acid-promoted reaction of a 1,2-diol. Protonation makes one hydroxyl group leave, then a 1,2 migration and carbonyl formation convert the diol into an aldehyde or ketone; intermediate stability guides the pathway.
